nazareth.d: A small hill village in lower Galilee where Jesus grew up. It overlooked the Jezreel Valley and the main road between the coast and the Jordan.

capernaum.d: Fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee and Jesus' base in Galilee. The ruins of a later synagogue stand on the foundations of the one he taught in.

bethsaida.d: Fishing town where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee. It was the home of Peter, Andrew and Philip, and the feeding of the 5,000 took place nearby.

chorazin.d: Hill town above Capernaum built of black basalt, one of the towns Jesus rebuked for not repenting.

magdala.d: Fish-processing town on the west shore of the lake and home of Mary Magdalene. A first-century synagogue was uncovered there in 2009.

tiberias.d: City built by Herod Antipas around AD 20 and named for the emperor Tiberius. It gave the Sea of Galilee its other name.

cana.m: Khirbet Qana or Kafr Kanna, Israel
cana.d: Galilean village where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding. It was also the home of Nathanael.

nain.d: Village on the slope of the Hill of Moreh where Jesus raised a widow's son.

tabor.d: Rounded mountain rising from the Jezreel Valley. Since the fourth century it has been honoured as the site of the transfiguration.

hermon.m: Mount Hermon, Israel, Syria and Lebanon
hermon.d: The highest mountain in the region, often snow-capped. Its snowmelt feeds the Jordan, and some think the transfiguration happened on its slopes.

galilee-sea.d: Freshwater lake about 21 by 13 kilometres, lying about 210 metres below sea level. Most of Jesus' ministry took place in the towns around its shores.

gerasenes.d: The steep east shore of the lake, in Gentile territory. Byzantine Christians built a monastery at Kursi to mark where the pigs rushed into the sea.

gadara.d: Greek city of the Decapolis on a ridge above the Yarmuk gorge, overlooking the Sea of Galilee.

caesarea-philippi.d: Town at a source of the Jordan beneath Mount Hermon, with a cave shrine to Pan. Here Peter confessed that Jesus is the Christ.

tyre.d: Ancient Phoenician island city famous for purple dye and sea trade. Alexander the Great joined it to the mainland with a causeway.

sidon.d: Phoenician port north of Tyre. Paul's ship stopped here on the voyage to Rome, and he was allowed to visit friends.

jordan.n: Jordan River at Bethany beyond the Jordan
jordan.m: Qasr al-Yahud and Al-Maghtas, on the Israel–Jordan border
jordan.d: The traditional place of Jesus' baptism, near where Israel crossed the Jordan under Joshua. It lies close to where the river enters the Dead Sea.

wilderness.d: Dry, rocky land falling steeply from Jerusalem to the Dead Sea. John preached here, and Jesus was tempted here for forty days.

jericho.d: Palm-tree oasis city near the Jordan and one of the oldest cities in the world. Herod built a winter palace here.

bethany.d: Village on the far slope of the Mount of Olives, about 3 kilometres from Jerusalem. It was the home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus.

olives.d: Ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, with Gethsemane at its foot. It was the scene of Jesus' entry into the city, his teaching on the end times and his ascension.

jerusalem.d: The holy city and site of the temple. It is the setting of Jesus' death and resurrection, Pentecost and the first church.

bethlehem.d: David's hometown, about 9 kilometres south of Jerusalem, where Jesus was born. The Church of the Nativity stands over a cave honoured since the second century.

emmaus.m: Traditional sites include el-Qubeibeh and Emmaus Nicopolis
emmaus.d: Village where two disciples recognised the risen Jesus as he broke bread. Luke places it about 11 kilometres from Jerusalem, and its exact site is debated.

sychar.d: Samaritan town near ancient Shechem, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Jacob's well is still in use.

samaria.d: Old capital of the northern kingdom, rebuilt by Herod and renamed Sebaste in honour of Augustus. Philip preached in the region of Samaria.

machaerus.d: Herod's hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea. Josephus says John the Baptist was imprisoned and executed there.

egypt.d: Roman province, rich in grain, with large Jewish communities in Alexandria and the Delta. The holy family found refuge here from Herod.

dead-sea.d: Salt lake at the lowest point on land, about 430 metres below sea level. Sodom and Gomorrah are traditionally placed near its southern end.

sodom.d: The cities of the plain destroyed in Abraham's day (Genesis 19). Their ruin was remembered as a warning of judgment.

megiddo.d: Fortress city guarding a pass into the Jezreel Valley, scene of many battles. 'Armageddon' comes from Har Megiddo, 'mount of Megiddo'.

sinai.d: The mountain where God gave Moses the law. St Catherine's Monastery has stood at its foot since the sixth century.

nineveh.d: Capital of Assyria on the Tigris. It repented at Jonah's preaching and fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.

petra.d: The Nabatean kingdom, with its capital at Petra, stretched east and south of Judea. Paul went to 'Arabia' after his conversion.

damascus.d: Ancient oasis city on the trade routes, with a large Jewish community. Paul met the risen Jesus on the road here.

gaza.d: Gaza was the last city before the desert road to Egypt. Philip met the Ethiopian official on this road.

joppa.d: Old port on the coast of Judea. Jonah sailed from here, Peter raised Tabitha here and saw the vision of the sheet here.

lydda.d: Town on the coastal plain where Peter healed Aeneas.

caesarea.d: Herod's grand harbour city and the seat of Roman governors. Cornelius lived here, and Paul was held here for two years.

ptolemais.d: Port north of Mount Carmel where Paul stayed a day with believers on his last journey to Jerusalem.

antioch.d: The third city of the empire, on the Orontes River. Believers were first called Christians here, and it was the base for Paul's journeys.

seleucia.d: Antioch's seaport, where Paul and Barnabas set sail for Cyprus.

tarsus.d: Paul's birthplace, a wealthy city of learning in Cilicia on the Cydnus River. Antony and Cleopatra met here.

salamis.d: Main port of eastern Cyprus, where Paul and Barnabas first preached in the synagogues.

paphos.d: Roman capital of Cyprus, where the governor Sergius Paulus believed.

perga.d: City in Pamphylia where John Mark left Paul and Barnabas to return to Jerusalem.

attalia.d: Harbour of Pamphylia from which Paul and Barnabas sailed home to Antioch.

pisidian-antioch.d: Roman colony on a high plateau in Galatia. Paul preached his first recorded sermon in its synagogue.

iconium.d: City on the plains of Galatia where Paul and Barnabas had to flee a plot to stone them.

lystra.d: Roman colony and Timothy's hometown. Paul was stoned and left for dead here.

derbe.d: The farthest town of Paul's first journey, where many became disciples.

galatia.d: Roman province in central Asia Minor, named for Celtic settlers. It included Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.

troas.d: Port near ancient Troy where Paul saw the vision of a man of Macedonia calling for help.

assos.d: Hilltop harbour town. Paul walked here from Troas while the others sailed around.

mitylene.d: Main city of the island of Lesbos, a stop on Paul's voyage to Jerusalem.

neapolis.d: Port of Philippi and Paul's first landing place in Europe.

philippi.d: Roman colony on the Via Egnatia, where Lydia believed and Paul and Silas sang in prison. It was the first church in Europe.

amphipolis.d: City on the Strymon River and the Via Egnatia that Paul passed through.

thessalonica.d: Capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the Via Egnatia. Paul planted a church here in a few weeks.

berea.d: Town whose Jews 'examined the Scriptures daily' to check Paul's message.

athens.d: The ancient centre of philosophy and art, full of temples. Paul spoke before the Areopagus council.

corinth.d: Rich Roman colony on the isthmus between two seas. Paul stayed 18 months and later wrote it at least two letters.

cenchreae.d: Corinth's eastern port and home of Phoebe, who probably carried Romans to Rome.

ephesus.d: Capital of the province of Asia and home of the temple of Artemis. Paul stayed nearly three years, and John is said to have lived here later.

miletus.d: Harbour city where Paul said a tearful farewell to the Ephesian elders.

cos.d: Island famous for its medical school founded by Hippocrates.

rhodes.d: Island and trading city once famous for the Colossus, a giant bronze statue that fell in an earthquake in 226 BC.

patara.d: Port in Lycia where Paul changed to a ship bound for Phoenicia.

myra.d: Lycian port where Paul's guard found an Alexandrian grain ship sailing for Italy.

cnidus.d: Cape at the tip of a long peninsula. Strong winds kept Paul's ship from going further west.

crete.d: Large island south of Greece. Titus was left here to appoint elders, and Paul's ship sheltered at Fair Havens on its south coast.

fair-havens.d: Small bay on Crete's south coast where Paul warned against sailing on.

malta.d: Island south of Sicily where Paul was shipwrecked. St Paul's Bay is the traditional site.

syracuse.d: Great city of Sicily, founded by Greeks, where Paul stayed three days.

rhegium.d: Port at the toe of Italy on the strait facing Sicily.

puteoli.d: Main port for grain ships from Egypt, near Naples. Paul found believers here.

appius.n: Forum of Appius and Three Taverns
appius.m: On the Appian Way south of Rome
appius.d: Stops on the Appian Way where believers from Rome came out to meet Paul.

rome.d: Capital of the empire with perhaps a million people. Paul and Peter are traditionally said to have been martyred here under Nero.

nicopolis.d: City founded by Augustus to celebrate his victory at Actium. Paul planned to spend a winter here.

colossae.d: Small town in the Lycus valley, home of Philemon and Onesimus. It has never been excavated.

laodicea.d: Wealthy banking city in the Lycus valley, known for black wool and eye salve. Its water came by aqueduct.

hierapolis.d: City of hot springs above white travertine terraces, near Laodicea and Colossae.

smyrna.d: Beautiful port city loyal to Rome. Its bishop Polycarp was martyred around AD 155.

pergamum.d: Hilltop city with a huge library, a famous altar to Zeus and the first temple to Augustus in Asia.

thyatira.d: Trading town with many guilds, including dyers. Lydia came from here.

sardis.d: Old capital of Lydia and rich King Croesus. Its 'unconquerable' citadel was captured twice by surprise.

philadelphia.d: Town on the edge of an earthquake zone, rebuilt after the great quake of AD 17.

patmos.d: Small rocky island where John was exiled and received the Revelation. The Cave of the Apocalypse is shown to visitors.

pontus.d: Province along the Black Sea coast, one of five regions 1 Peter was sent to.

cappadocia.d: High plateau province in Asia Minor. Jews from here were in Jerusalem at Pentecost.

bithynia.d: Province on the Sea of Marmara. Its governor Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan about Christians around AD 112.

euphrates.d: The great river of Mesopotamia and the eastern edge of the Roman Empire.

patmos-churches.d: The seven churches lay on a ring road through the province of Asia: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea.
